candidate_relations.reason: Sequential bilateral MCA infarcts are consequences of the microangiopathy rather than the hematologic diagnosis itself.
Normal coagulation studies despite thrombocytopenia and hemolysis argue against disseminated intravascular coagulation.
No lupus clinical features or serology are provided to explain the thrombotic microangiopathy.
The case has microangiopathic hemolysis with schistocytes rather than documented antiphospholipid antibodies or large-vessel thrombosis.
Thrombocytopenia was present at admission without preceding heparin exposure.
Prominent neurologic ischemia with no reported renal failure favors TTP over atypical HUS.
No hemoglobinuria, pancytopenia, or flow-cytometric PNH clone was reported.
Falling platelets, Coombs-negative hemolysis, and schistocytes establish TMA without naming the TTP subtype.
A 59-year-old with normal limb anatomy and newly falling platelets cannot have thrombocytopenia-absent-radius syndrome.
Severe thrombocytopenia, Coombs-negative microangiopathic hemolysis, neurologic decline, and normal coagulation fit TTP.
The preserved coagulation profile conflicts with DIC despite elevated inflammatory markers and D-dimer.
Bilateral evolving cerebral infarcts accompanied platelet nadir 21×10^3/μL, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, high LDH, and schistocytes.
Hemoglobin was initially 15 g/dL and no sickling history or electrophoresis evidence is given.
Both direct and indirect Coombs tests were negative, opposing immune hemolysis in Evans syndrome.
The presentation was neurologic with no kidney injury or diarrheal prodrome documented for HUS.
CT confirmed right and then left MCA ischemic strokes, which do not encompass the systemic blood disorder.
Schistocytes, LDH 1148 U/L, and indirect bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL define MAHA but omit thrombocytopenic TTP.
HUS is an alternate TMA, but absent renal failure and dominant cerebral events make its subtype incompatible.

case_quality_flags: ADAMTS13 activity is not reported, although the clinical and laboratory pattern strongly supports the reference diagnosis.
